titre: AI Adoption, Adaptation, and Workforce Sustainability in Medical Imaging: Systematic Review and Conceptual Framework.
auteurs: Brough P, Zobair KM, Pool J, Haskell N, Houghton L, Scuffham P, Loy J, Troth A, Memon S, Smithson R, Khan M, Murphy B, Living L, Du L, Richards J, Dolkens J, Aitken M, Zhang J, Grieve J, Bhuta S.
resume: Background Despite growing recognition that AI-driven systems offer transformative benefits for diagnostic imaging, insufficient evidence exists regarding how medical imaging workforces adapt to AI technology to support workforce sustainability. Objective The aim of this study is to systematically review the existing literature on perceptions and attitudes toward AI adoption in medical imaging, postadoption adaptation behaviors within the workforce, and the implications of these processes for workforce sustainability. Methods Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, a systematic search was carried out across 7 databases. Thematic analysis was used to systematically identify, analyze, and interpret patterns across the literature, providing a comprehensive understanding of workforce perceptions and adaptation behaviors. Results A total of 69 peer-reviewed articles were included for thematic synthesis. The findings produced 6 critical factors that were identified as themes associated with AI adoption: perceived benefits, trust, readiness to change, autonomy and control, perceived threat to professional identity, and attitudes and intentions toward AI adoption and use. Four key facets of effective cognitive and behavioral adaptation were identified: training and skills development, task performance during AI-assisted practice, reduction of mental health burden and work strain, and policy compliance. The influence of work engagement and job satisfaction on workforce sustainability was also conceptualized. The findings were integrated into a framework describing the radiology workforce perspectives on AI adoption, adaptation behaviors, and workforce sustainability. Conclusions The findings have potential implications for policy, particularly in strengthening AI-equipped medical imaging systems, fostering trust in AI-driven technologies, and supporting workforce training and upskilling, while considering professional autonomy and role identity. The review highlights a research gap, emphasizing the need for further investigation into postadoption adaptation processes and informing policy development that links AI integration with long-term workforce sustainability in medical imaging.

titre: Advances in Machine Learning Paradigms for Reliable Swimming Pool Drowning Detection: Systematic Review of Methods and Implementations.
auteurs: Chepkorir M, Orowe I, Abade E, Kamanu T.
resume: Background Drowning is a leading cause of unintentional injury-related mortality worldwide, particularly in swimming pool environments, where rapid detection is critical to prevent fatalities. Traditional monitoring approaches rely on lifeguards and rule-based systems, which are often limited by human error, delayed response, and environmental challenges such as occlusion, glare, and multiple swimmers. Machine learning (ML) and computer vision methods have emerged as promising alternatives for automated drowning detection; however, their methodological rigor, real-world applicability, and reliability remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to systematically review advancements in ML-based drowning detection systems over the past 15 years. The review focused on detection methods, sensing modalities, evaluation metrics, and validation practices. It also examined how studies addressed real-world challenges such as occlusion, lighting variability, and multiswimmer environments, and identified key gaps related to generalizability, reliability, and privacy. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted using major electronic databases, including IEEE Xplore, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar. A total of 4927 records were initially identified and screened by 2 independent reviewers using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. A final set of 30 studies was included for data extraction and synthesis. The methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST), while reporting transparency was evaluated using the TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis) guidelines. Data analysis was conducted in R. Results The findings indicate that drowning detection research is dominated by supervised, vision-based approaches (23/30, 76.7%), with convolutional neural networks (5/30, 16.7%) and You Only Look Once-based architectures (7/30, 23.3%) being the most commonly used methods. While reported performance is generally high, with mean accuracy exceeding 90.9%, evaluation practices are heavily centered on accuracy, with limited reporting of precision, recall, false alarm rate, and latency. One of 30 (3.3%) studies reported validation under real-world operational conditions, with an additional 5 (16.7%) studies using real-world data without formal real-world validation, and no studies conducted cross-dataset evaluation. In addition, critical real-world challenges such as occlusion, glare, and crowding were rarely addressed ( Conclusions ML-based drowning detection systems have demonstrated substantial progress in algorithm development, particularly in vision-based models. However, this progress is not matched by equivalent advances in validation, robustness, and real-world applicability. The field is characterized by a significant gap between experimental performance and deployment readiness. Future research should prioritize standardized evaluation frameworks, external validation, comprehensive performance reporting, and the integration of multimodal and privacy-preserving approaches to enable reliable real-world implementation.

titre: AI-Enabled Digital Health Tool Implementation in Clinical Practice Settings: Umbrella Review.
auteurs: Gilbert A, Gacad A, Parrish L, Nguyen O, Turner K, Tarver WL, Jonnalagadda P, Tsagli D, Wu B, Lu C, Sachs RE, Evbuomwan O, Kepper MK.
resume: Background AI has the potential to improve clinical decision-making, efficiency, and patient outcomes, yet adoption in routine clinical practice has been slower than anticipated. While prior studies have identified factors that influence AI implementation, a comprehensive synthesis grounded in implementation science frameworks is lacking. Objective This study aimed to qualitatively and comprehensively describe barriers and facilitators to AI implementation in clinical care settings using an implementation science determinants framework, the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), and to identify AI-specific determinants not fully captured by CFIR. Methods We conducted an umbrella review of reviews examining determinants of AI implementation in clinical practice. In accordance with the PRIOR (Preferred Reporting Items for Overviews of Reviews) reporting guidance, we systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL for English-language reviews published between January 2013 and July 2025. Reviews were included if they addressed barriers to and facilitators of implementing AI-enabled digital health tools in clinical care settings. Determinants were deductively mapped to the updated CFIR and inductively analyzed to identify emergent AI-specific constructs. Review quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist, and overlap among primary studies was evaluated using the GROOVE (Graphical Representation of Overlap for Overviews) tool. Results Twenty-two reviews published between 2021 and 2025 were included, encompassing studies conducted from 1990 to 2025. Reviews varied in design, including systematic, scoping, rapid, narrative, and literature reviews. Overall review quality was mixed, with 9 (41%) reviews rated at 100% quality and 4 (18%) at 50% or lower. Primary study overlap was slight, with a corrected covered area of 0.4%. Determinants of AI implementation were identified across all CFIR domains. Prominent barriers at the innovation level included limited evidence of clinical impact, poor interpretability, complexity, lack of adaptability, and insufficiently representative data. Facilitators included perceived relative advantage, co-design with clinicians, and evidence of local clinical benefit. At the implementer level, low AI literacy, limited confidence, time constraints, and concerns about professional displacement were common barriers, while training and technical support facilitated adoption. Inner setting barriers included inadequate infrastructure, limited resources, poor workflow compatibility, and weak governance structures. Outer setting barriers included unclear policies, laws, and liability frameworks, whereas partnerships and cross-sector collaboration were frequent facilitators. Inductively identified AI-specific determinants included transparency, trust, accountability, model bias, data governance, model maintenance, robustness, generalizability, existential threat, and concern about loss of the human element in care. Conclusions AI implementation in clinical settings is shaped by complex, multilevel, and AI-specific determinants that extend beyond traditional digital health considerations. Implementation science frameworks can be adapted to incorporate these constructs. Tailored, theory-informed strategies addressing technical, organizational, psychological, and regulatory factors are essential to support safe, equitable, and sustainable integration of AI into clinical care.

titre: Artificial intelligence-assisted microdissection testicular sperm extraction improves sperm retrieval efficiency and clinical outcomes in men with non-obstructive azoospermia: a retrospective cohort study.
resume: This study compared the efficacy, safety, and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) outcomes of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted versus conventional microdissection testicular sperm extraction (micro-TESE) in men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA). To this end, we retrospectively analyzed 1286 consecutive NOA patients undergoing micro-TESE at the two reproductive medicine center of Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital (Chengdu, China) and Sichuan Jinxin Xinan Women's and Children's Hospital (Chengdu, China) from January 2020 to December 2024, including 542 patients receiving AI-assisted procedures and 744 undergoing conventional surgery. The primary outcome was sperm retrieval rate (SRR), while secondary outcomes covered intraoperative parameters, postoperative complications, and ICSI outcomes, and univariable and multivariable logistic regression were performed to identify independent predictors of SRR and live birth. The results showed that the overall SRR reached 56.2% in the entire cohort, and the AI group had a significantly higher SRR (68.1% vs 47.6%, P < 0.001), with the most prominent improvement observed in patients with Sertoli cell-only syndrome (47.2% vs 22.7%, P < 0.001). The AI group also exhibited shorter operative time, less intraoperative blood loss, fewer biopsy sites, shorter postoperative hospital stay, and lower complication rates (all P < 0.001), as well as superior ICSI outcomes including higher fertilization, high-quality embryo, blastocyst, clinical pregnancy, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth rates (all P < 0.01). Further multivariable analysis confirmed that AI-assisted surgery serves as an independent predictor of both successful SRR (odds ratio [OR] = 3.182, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.374-4.265, P < 0.001) and live birth rate (OR = 1.876, 95% CI: 1.325-2.656, P < 0.001). Taken together, AI-assisted micro-TESE improves sperm retrieval efficiency, reduces perioperative morbidity, and enhances ICSI and live birth outcomes in NOA patients as an independent predictor for both SRR and live birth rate, and prospective multicenter randomized trials are warranted for further validation.

titre: American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification: Hybrid Machine Learning-Large Language Model Ensemble Retrospective Validation Study.
auteurs: Pabalan C, Stewart A, Fisher G, Fisher A.
resume: Background The American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status (ASA-PS) classification system fundamentally shapes perioperative care delivery but suffers from poor interrater reliability (0.4-0.6). Machine learning (ML) models and large language models (LLMs) offer complementary remedies: ML processes structured data consistently but cannot interpret the nuance of clinical narratives, while LLMs parse narrative text and generate explanations but adhere inconsistently to diagnostic criteria. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate a parallel ML-LLM ensemble that combines the complementary strengths of both approaches for automated ASA-PS classification. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 3000 adult surgical encounters from the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences (UAMS) between August 2024 and May 2025. Cases were randomly allocated to training (n=2000), validation (N=500), and held-out test sets (N=500). The validation set was used exclusively for architecture comparison and hyperparameter tuning, and the held-out test set was reserved for final model performance validation. We developed multiple architectures, including traditional ML models (Extreme Gradient Boosting [XGBoost], Light Gradient Boosting Machine [LightGBM], ExtraTrees), an LLM-only baseline (Generative Pretrained Transformer-4o [GPT-4o]), and hybrid approaches. The parallel ensemble processed structured data through XGBoost and unstructured clinical notes through GPT-4o independently, with outputs combined via weighted averaging. Model performance was evaluated using macro- F 1 -score, exact match accuracy, and ±1-class accuracy. Results A theoretical performance ceiling of macro- F 1 -score=0.59 was determined through evaluation by an expert panel of 2 board-certified anesthesiologists (AF and GF) who independently rated 50 patient charts for ASA-PS scores. On the true held-out test set (N=500), the parallel ensemble ( α =0.30) achieved a macro- F 1 -score of 0.530 (95% CI 0.350-0.600), exact match accuracy of 0.630 (95% CI 0.580-0.670), and ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968-0.992), exceeding the frozen LLM-only baseline evaluated on the same set (macro- F 1 -score 0.493, exact match accuracy 0.621,±1-class accuracy 0.981). On the validation set used for architecture selection, the ensemble outperformed structured-only ML (XGBoost macro- F 1 -score=0.333, P F 1 -score of 0.642 (95% CI 0.525-0.691), nominally exceeding the expert panel ceiling. Per-class analysis attributed this to a perfect score on the 2 validation ASA-PS 5 cases. Excluding that class, the adjusted macro- F 1 -score was approximately 0.55, within the range of the parallel ensemble. The LLM component also generated explanations detailing comorbidities, severity descriptors, and functional status indicators. Conclusions The parallel ML-LLM ensemble achieved performance approaching the theoretical ceiling established by the expert panel benchmark while providing interpretable clinical explanations. The ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968-0.992) may enhance operational safety by minimizing extreme misclassifications. This approach demonstrates how complementary AI architectures can enhance perioperative risk assessment, which is particularly valuable given current health care workforce shortages.

titre: AI feedback for clinician assessment of umbilical and middle cerebral artery Doppler ultrasound: a multicenter randomized trial.
revue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
auteurs: Bashir Z, Wong CK, Lin M, Raheli A, Feragen A, Christensen AN, Pehrson C, Nielsen M, Andreasen L, Andersen BR, Eggers AGH, Tolsgaard MG.
resume: Background Assessment accuracy for umbilical artery (UA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler ultrasound assessment depends on operator expertise. Artificial intelligence (AI) based feedback may improve performance, but its effect on assessment accuracy and the role of clinical experience remain uncertain. Objective To determine whether AI feedback improves assessment accuracy for standardized image-based umbilical artery and middle cerebral artery Doppler vignettes among novice and experienced clinicians. Study design This multicenter randomized clinical trial was conducted at five Danish hospitals. Ninety-six clinicians from obstetrics and gynecology departments, including residents, gynecologists, and obstetricians, were randomized 1:1 to AI-generated visual and textual feedback or no AI feedback. Each clinician evaluated 40 standardized image-based Doppler vignettes containing pre-existing static UA and MCA Doppler images. In total, 1,920 unique Doppler vignettes were evaluated across 48 clinician pairs matched by obstetric ultrasound experience. For color Doppler vignettes, clinicians indicated intended gate placement; for spectral Doppler vignettes, they judged waveform technical adequacy. Both are essential components of a technically valid Doppler measurement. No real-time scanning was performed. Intervention clinicians viewed the unannotated image alongside artificial intelligence feedback on gate placement, anatomical suitability, insonation angle, and spectral waveform quality, then entered their own response on the unannotated image. Accuracy was determined by expert consensus using predefined International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology-based criteria. AI feedback was classified as correct or incorrect according to whether it agreed with expert consensus. Expert consensus was based on two fetal medicine sonographers with >10 years of obstetric ultrasound experience, with disagreements resolved by a fetal medicine consultant. Clinicians were classified as novices ( Results Overall assessment accuracy was higher with AI feedback than without (75.0% vs 62.3%; mean difference, 12.7%; 95% CI, 8.2-17.1; p Conclusion AI feedback improved assessment accuracy for standardized umbilical artery and middle cerebral artery Doppler vignettes among novice and experienced clinicians. Clinical experience remained important when AI feedback was incorrect, supporting further evaluation of human-artificial intelligence collaboration during real-time Doppler acquisition.
